name: Manitoba
summary_text: Manitoba stands under the national framework: Canada is among the safer large destinations for trans visitors, with gender identity and gender expression protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16 in 2017. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.  Provincially, the Manitoba Human Rights Code already prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The NDP government has a bill before the Legislative Assembly to extend the Code to gender expression as well. Justice Minister Matt Wiebe says the change would align Manitoba with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward presentation such as clothing. The bill was slated for debate later in 2025, and Charlie Eau, executive director of Trans Manitoba, welcomed it. Until it passes, gender expression is not itself a listed prohibited ground in Manitoba, though conduct based on gender identity remains covered.  Manitoba's recorded hate-crime exposure is low by national standards. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, a 1% rise on 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba recorded a rate of 5.3 per 100,000, joint-lowest among the provinces with Newfoundland and Labrador, and no increase in 2024, placing it among the eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly across the country, and police figures capture only incidents reported to and recorded by police. Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an LGBTIQ+ organisation's reading of the same national police data, breaks out gender identity as a motivation alongside sexual orientation.  Provincial recognition of trans Manitobans is enacted and dated. The Legislative Assembly passed a bill on 30 May 2024 recognising March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender. Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported.  The government also marks Transgender Day of Remembrance publicly. On 20 November 2023 the transgender flag was raised in Memorial Park in Winnipeg, an observance the province first held eight years earlier, with the flag raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara said in a statement that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia and that such violence shows no sign of slowing.

name: New Brunswick
summary_text: Visitors in New Brunswick stand under the Canadian national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.  Provincial education policy is the layer where New Brunswick differs from the rest of Canada. Policy 713 (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity) of the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development took effect on 17 August 2020, was revised on 1 July and 23 August 2023, and was revised again effective 1 January 2025. Under the current text, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them informally in school, with parental consent encouraged but not required; formal use of a chosen name in official records for a student under 16 still requires parental consent. The revision was made by the Holt government and goes beyond the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.  The application clause of Policy 713 covers the school environment as a whole and names the people it binds: all students, school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors. A non-resident present in a New Brunswick classroom, whether as a visiting professional, student teacher or volunteer, is therefore subject to the same name, pronoun and privacy rules as a pupil.  The 2023 revisions remain the reference point for what the province is capable of imposing. Changes taking effect on 1 July 2023 barred teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropped explicit wording permitting students to take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, in accordance with their gender identity. The Progressive Conservative government of Premier Blaine Higgs made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers resigned in protest and two others were removed, eight party members including six cabinet ministers boycotted question period over the handling of the file, and dissidents called for a leadership review. The Holt government's 1 January 2025 revision undoes the 2023 consent rule, which had drawn protests outside the legislature and a constitutional challenge by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.  Facilities are addressed by Policy 713 as originally written: the 2020 policy requires schools to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Whether that requirement survives verbatim in the text revised on 1 January 2025 is not established by the sources.  In federal custody, the Correctional Service of Canada permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution matching their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on their identification documents. Requests are assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved overriding health or safety concern exists under the service's 2022 gender-diversity policy. As of 2025 the service recorded 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's; between fiscal years 2017-18 and 2024-25 it received 129 requests from people assigned male at birth for placement in women's institutions, with 35 approved, 72 denied and 22 withdrawn. The Correctional Investigator has criticised the unclear health-or-safety override and the absence of a dedicated abuse-reporting mechanism. This federal policy is the framework a trans person in federal custody in New Brunswick stands under.
